title: Quentin and the Portrait
premise: Rosalind Kavanagh, a pest controller with a hard rule against the supernatural, is hired to deal with 'something with fingerprints' in the derelict Kestrel House, where a portrait of a hanged ancestor watches every room. When an excavation crew unearths a cellar door sealed from the inside, Rosalind discovers the house's founding family survived on a bargain: each generation must learn and sing the song's last verse to keep what's buried below asleep. The verse was lost when the last heir burned the family papers, and now the thing below is learning to knock. Rosalind, whose own grandmother was the Kavanaghs' loyal housekeeper, must choose between exposing the inheritance of guilt that kept her family complicit for a century and finishing the verse herself—she reconstructs it from her grandmother's lullabies, sings it at the door as it opens, and survives by refusing the final line, sealing the thing away but leaving the debt unpaid and the portrait's eyes open.
about_author: Ada Winterbourne is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate sales and unclaimed inheritances in northern England. She writes horror about the paperwork of old sins and the families that sign for them.

chapters.title: Something with Fingerprints
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Called to Kestrel House over reports of greasy handprints climbing the interior walls at night, Rosalind finds prints that match no living resident—too long, too many joints. She sets traps, names it vermin, and refuses the caretaker's talk of the portrait. Emotional beat: professional skepticism established as armor, already cracking at the edges.

chapters.title: The Portrait Watches Back
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Working alone after dark, she notices the hanged man in the ancestral portrait has changed posture since her last visit—and that the fingerprints always appear beneath his frame. A locked drawer yields a hymnal with the last page torn out. Emotional beat: dread replaces annoyance; her rule against believing meets its first real test.

chapters.title: The Excavation Crew
chapters.summary: POV Dev, crew foreman and Rosalind's ex. His team, hired to dig foundations for the house's conversion, breaks through a cellar floor and finds a door—oak, iron-banded, sealed from the inside with wax and hair. That night his youngest worker scratches at his own window from within. Emotional beat: the outside world is pulled into the haunting; guilt begins spreading like an infection.

chapters.title: Sealed from the Inside
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. She and Dev examine the door: whoever built it wanted to keep something in, not out, and the seal is renewed generationally. In parish records she finds the pattern—the Kestrels paid one family, the Kavanaghs, to 'keep the singing' for a hundred years. Her grandmother's name is in the ledger. Emotional beat: betrayal; her family's loyalty was complicity.

chapters.title: The Verse That Was Burned
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The last Kestrel heir, dying in 1974, burned the papers containing the song's final verse rather than pass on the burden—or so the record claims. Knocking begins under the floorboards, patient, rhythmic, matching the meter of the incomplete hymnal. Emotional beat: rising panic as the abstract becomes audible.

chapters.title: Loyalty Is a Kind of Lie
chapters.summary: POV Dev. One of his crew, Marcus, stops sleeping and starts humming a tune none of them taught him. Dev finds Rosalind's grandmother's letters hidden in the chapel wall: the Kavanaghs knew everything and stayed silent for wages and protection. He confronts Rosalind with them. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth made explicit between the two leads; their old rupture reopens along the same fault line.

chapters.title: What the Lullabies Kept
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Grieving and furious, she listens back through memory: her grandmother's lullabies were the verse, disguised, sung to her every childhood night. She transcribes it and realizes the final line is missing—not torn out, never written down, because it must be refused aloud. Emotional beat: reluctant inheritance accepted; the theme of justice outside the law sharpens—the law here is the bargain, and she means to break it.

chapters.title: The House Stops Pretending
chapters.summary: POV alternating Rosalind/Dev. The excavation site collapses inward; the portrait's rope creaks though nothing moves; Marcus walks into the cellar and starts singing the found verses in a voice not his. The knocking becomes pounding. Emotional beat: full escalation, the house dropping its mask, allies scattered and desperate.

chapters.title: The Last Verse Without Singing Along
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. At the opening door, Rosalind sings the reconstructed verse while the thing below offers her the final line in her grandmother's voice—an easy ending, a clean inheritance. She carries the melody to its edge and refuses the words, closing the seal with her own silence where the line should be. Emotional beat: climax; justice done outside any lawful bargain, at personal cost.

chapters.title: Eyes Open
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind, weeks later. The house stands, the crew recovers, the portrait hangs in a museum crate—but its eyes remain open, and Rosalind sometimes hums the tune without meaning to, stopping just short of the end. The debt is deferred, not forgiven. Emotional beat: quiet, unresolved resolution; loyalty to the dead transformed into vigilance toward the living.
